analogy.p: Think of a device like a package that has travelled the world before you ever open it. Digging up the metals is the first leg, building it is the second, and shipping it is the third. Using it is the quiet middle, and throwing it away is the final stretch that can leave a mess if nobody collects the rubbish. Just as a journey's real fuel cost includes the trip to the airport and the empty return flight, a device's real cost includes everything before and after the screen lights up. The analogy breaks down because a journey ends when you arrive, whereas a device's materials can be recovered and sent round again by recycling.
analogy.t: A device is like a long-distance journey with hidden costs

bullets: Impacts happen at **every stage**: raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and disposal.
The impact can be **negative** (pollution, resource use, waste) or **positive** (reduced travel, less paper, smarter use of energy).
Exam questions usually give a **scenario** (a school buying tablets, a company with a data centre, a phone upgrade) and expect you to apply the ideas to it.
The command word 'discuss' means you must give **both sides** and then a judgement.
Environmental issues link to **ethical** issues, because the harm often falls on people in other countries.
Link to other topics: the **digital divide** and **legislation** (for example rules on disposing of electrical equipment) also appear in section 1.6.
core.h: What 'environmental impact' means in this topic
core.p: The OCR specification asks you to consider the impact of digital technology on the **environment** alongside ethical, legal, cultural and privacy issues. 'Environmental impact' means the effect that making, using and throwing away technology has on the natural world: the land, water, air, wildlife and climate. Digital technology is often thought of as 'clean' because it has no smoke or exhaust, but every device is made from physical materials, runs on electricity that is usually generated somewhere, and eventually becomes waste. A strong answer looks at the **whole life of a device**, not just the moment it is switched on.

bullets: Mining **destroys habitats** and can cause soil erosion and loss of biodiversity.
Extraction and refining uses **a lot of energy**, often from fossil fuels, producing carbon dioxide.
Chemicals used in processing can **contaminate water supplies**.
Some materials are **rare or finite**; using more devices uses up limited resources.
Mining conditions in some regions raise **ethical** concerns for workers and local communities.
Recycling recovered metals **reduces the need for new mining**, which is why recycling matters.
Exam tip: use the phrase **finite resources** rather than just 'running out'.
core.p: Digital devices are built from many materials that have to be **mined or extracted** from the Earth. Smartphones, laptops and servers contain metals such as **copper, gold, silver, aluminium, lithium and cobalt**, plus plastics made from oil. Mining removes habitats, uses large amounts of water and energy, and can pollute rivers and soil with chemicals. Some of these materials are **finite (non-renewable)**, which means they cannot be replaced once used up, so building more devices than we need uses up resources that future generations may need.

bullets: Factories use **large amounts of electricity**, often generated by burning fossil fuels.
Production uses **water and chemicals**, which can cause pollution if not controlled.
The **carbon footprint** (total greenhouse gases released) is built in before the device is ever switched on.
Short **product lifecycles** and annual upgrades mean more manufacturing and more waste.
Some manufacturers practise **planned obsolescence**: designing products so they become outdated or hard to repair.
Better design (repairable, upgradeable, long-lasting) **reduces the demand for new manufacturing**.
Packaging and transport add further **emissions**.
core.p: Turning raw materials into processors, screens, batteries and circuit boards needs **energy-hungry, highly controlled factories**. Chip manufacture in particular uses large amounts of electricity and very clean water, and produces chemical waste that must be handled carefully. For many everyday devices such as phones, a **large share of their lifetime carbon footprint comes from manufacture**, not from the electricity used when you charge them. This is why keeping a device for longer is usually better for the environment than upgrading every year.

bullets: Moving parts and finished goods around the world uses **fossil fuels**.
Greenhouse gases such as **carbon dioxide** trap heat and contribute to **global warming**.
Air freight has a **higher footprint** than sea freight.
Packaging materials add **waste and emissions**.
Local sourcing and consolidated deliveries can **reduce** the impact.
Do not over-explain this stage in the exam; it is a supporting point rather than the main one.
core.p: Components are often made in several countries and shipped to be assembled, then sent again to warehouses and shops or directly to customers. Transport by ship, aeroplane and lorry burns fuel and releases **carbon dioxide**, which is a **greenhouse gas** that contributes to **climate change**. Online shopping adds delivery vehicles and returns. Although transport is usually a smaller part of a device's footprint than manufacturing, it is part of the full life-cycle picture and is worth a mention in a developed answer.

bullets: Devices use electricity in **normal use and on standby**.
If the electricity comes from **fossil fuels**, using it releases carbon dioxide.
Larger, more powerful devices (gaming PCs, big screens) generally **use more power**.
Settings such as **sleep mode, auto-off and lower screen brightness** reduce consumption.
Choosing devices with a good **energy efficiency rating** reduces running costs and emissions.
Using **renewable energy** (wind, solar, hydroelectric) lowers the carbon cost of each unit of electricity.
Link to cost: saving energy also **saves money**, which gives organisations a reason to act.
core.h: Stage 4: energy use while devices are running
core.p: Every device uses **electricity** when it is on or on standby, and a great deal of the world's electricity is still generated from **fossil fuels** such as coal and gas. Using more electricity therefore usually means releasing more **carbon dioxide**. Devices that are left on standby, screens that stay lit, and equipment that is constantly running all add up, particularly across a whole school, company or country. Energy-efficient design, sleep modes and powering devices from **renewable energy** (wind, solar, hydroelectric) all reduce this impact.

bullets: Data centres contain **thousands of servers** running continuously.
Servers generate **heat**, so cooling uses extra electricity and water (see the data-centre figure).
Cloud storage, streaming, online gaming and large file transfers all **increase demand**.
Operators can use **renewable energy**, locate in cooler climates and use **efficient cooling**.
Waste heat can sometimes be **reused**, for example to heat nearby buildings.
Using the cloud is not 'free of impact': the impact has simply **moved out of sight**.
Deleting unused files and avoiding unnecessary streaming in high definition **reduces demand**.
core.h: Data centres, the internet and the cloud
core.p: The internet and **cloud storage** depend on huge buildings full of servers called **data centres**. Servers run 24 hours a day and produce a lot of heat, so data centres also need **cooling systems** that use more electricity and often water. Every email stored, video streamed, photo backed up or website visited uses some of this energy somewhere. Because so many people now stream, game and store data online, the energy demand of data centres and networks is a major environmental concern. Companies try to reduce it by using renewable power, more efficient servers and smarter cooling.

bullets: **E-waste** is discarded electrical and electronic equipment.
Contains **toxic substances** that can leak from landfill into soil and water.
Burning cables or batteries releases **harmful fumes** that damage health and air quality.
Valuable metals are **lost** if devices are dumped instead of recycled.
Some e-waste is **exported** to poorer countries where unsafe recycling harms workers: an **ethical** issue as well.
Lithium batteries can cause **fires** if damaged or crushed in waste facilities.
Short upgrade cycles and difficulty of repair **increase the quantity** of e-waste.
core.p: When devices are thrown away they become **electronic waste (e-waste)**, one of the fastest-growing types of waste in the world. Electronic equipment contains **hazardous substances** such as lead, mercury, cadmium and flame retardants. If devices end up in **landfill** or are burned or dismantled without proper protection, these chemicals can leak into the soil and groundwater and harm wildlife and people. E-waste also contains valuable materials like gold and copper that are wasted if the device is not recycled.

bullets: **Reduce**: only buy what you need; choose durable, repairable, upgradeable products.
**Reuse**: repair, donate to schools or charities, sell on, or pass to family.
**Recycle**: take to a proper recycling centre or return to the retailer or manufacturer so valuable materials are recovered.
Reuse is generally **better than recycling** because it needs no further processing.
Recycling **reduces landfill** and the need for new mining.
Manufacturers can offer **take-back schemes** and design products to be easy to dismantle.
Governments set **laws and targets** for collecting and recycling electrical waste in the UK.
core.p: The best way to cut environmental harm is to follow the idea of **reduce, reuse, recycle**. **Reducing** means buying fewer devices and keeping them longer. **Reusing** means repairing, upgrading, selling or donating devices so they have a second life. **Recycling** means breaking devices down properly so that metals and plastics can be recovered and used again. Recycling saves raw materials and energy compared with mining and manufacturing from scratch, but it still needs energy and is not perfect, which is why reuse comes first.

bullets: **Remote working and video calls** cut commuting and business travel emissions.
**Paperless offices** and digital documents reduce paper, printing and transport.
**Smart meters and smart heating** let people monitor and reduce energy use.
**Sensors and data** help farms use less water and fertiliser and help cities manage traffic.
**Computer modelling** supports climate science and the design of efficient products.
Online services can replace **physical shops, CDs and DVDs**, though streaming has its own energy cost.
Benefits depend on people actually **changing behaviour**, for example not printing the documents anyway.
core.h: How technology can reduce environmental harm
core.p: Digital technology is not only a cause of environmental problems; it can also help to **solve** them. Video conferencing and remote working mean fewer car and plane journeys. Digital documents, e-books and online forms **reduce the use of paper**. Smart thermostats and smart meters help people use less energy at home. Sensors, data analysis and computer models help scientists track climate change, forecast weather, manage traffic and design more efficient engines and buildings. These benefits can be larger than the technology's own footprint, depending on how it is used.

bullets: Use the structure **Point, Explain, Link to the scenario** for each idea.
Always include **at least one positive and one negative** in a 'discuss' answer.
Finish with a short **conclusion**: 'Overall, ... because ...'.
Weighing words to use: **however, on the other hand, whereas, depends on, outweighs**.
Specific examples score better than vague statements such as 'it is bad for the planet'.
Do not just list; **explain the cause and effect** (for example 'servers produce heat, so cooling uses more electricity').
Keep ethical and legal points separate unless the question links them.
core.h: Comparing positive and negative impacts: building a balanced answer
core.p: Higher-mark questions ask you to **discuss** or **evaluate**, which means weighing both sides. A balanced answer names a harm, explains **why** it happens, names a benefit, explains why it helps, and then gives a **judgement** that depends on the scenario. For example, a company switching to remote working saves travel but increases home energy use and relies on data centres. The key is to link each point to the **scenario in the question** and to say whether the overall effect is likely to be positive or negative and why.

bullets: **Individuals**: reuse, repair, recycle, switch off, choose efficient products.
**Businesses**: sustainable design, renewable power, take-back schemes, ethical sourcing.
**Governments**: regulations, targets, recycling centres and incentives.
In the UK, electrical waste should not go in ordinary household bins; it should go to **designated collection points** or be taken back by retailers.
Consumers can push companies to improve by choosing **greener products**.
This links to **ethical and legal** issues, which are also part of section 1.6.
Responsibilities overlap, so the best answers show how they **work together**.
core.h: Who is responsible? Individuals, businesses and governments
core.p: Reducing the environmental impact of technology is a shared responsibility. **Individuals** can buy fewer devices, repair them, switch off equipment and recycle properly. **Businesses** can design longer-lasting products, use renewable energy, run efficient data centres and offer take-back and recycling schemes. **Governments** can pass laws, such as regulations requiring electrical waste to be collected and recycled, set energy-efficiency standards and provide recycling facilities. Mentioning more than one group, and linking to the scenario, helps you reach the higher mark bands.

bullets: School scenario: **donate or recycle** old computers; buy **energy-efficient** replacements.
Company scenario: cloud servers still use energy, but **shared, efficient data centres** may use less than many small server rooms.
Phone scenario: keeping the phone longer **cuts manufacturing demand and e-waste**.
Smart city scenario: sensors save energy but must be **made, powered and eventually disposed of**.
Always say **who is affected**: people, wildlife, future generations.
Always give a **reduction method**: reuse, recycle, renewable energy, efficient design.
Check that your final sentence answers the **specific question** asked.
core.h: Putting it together: scenarios you might be given
core.p: Exam questions turn the theory into everyday contexts. A **school replacing its computers** raises e-waste, the option to donate or recycle old machines, and the energy rating of new ones. A **company moving to the cloud** raises data centre energy use against the savings of not running its own servers. A **person upgrading their phone every year** raises manufacturing footprint, mining and e-waste. A **town introducing smart street lighting** raises energy saving against the manufacture of the sensors. For each, think: where does the impact occur, who is affected, and what could reduce it?

exam: **State/Give/Identify (1 mark)**: one short fact, for example 'Data centres use a lot of electricity'. No explanation needed.
**Describe (2 marks)**: make a point and add a detail, for example 'E-waste contains toxic chemicals (1) which can leak into the soil from landfill (1)'.
**Explain (2 to 4 marks)**: each mark is a point plus a reason; use the word **because** or **so that**.
**Give two environmental impacts**: name two separate ideas, such as mining of finite resources and energy used by data centres; do not repeat the same idea in different words.
**Discuss (6 marks)**: include benefits **and** harms, link to the scenario, and end with a judgement; written in sentences, this is marked on level of response.
**Level-of-response tip**: a top-band answer is balanced, uses technical terms (e-waste, carbon dioxide, finite resources, renewable energy) and applies them to the scenario.
**Suggest ways to reduce**: reuse and donate, recycle at proper collection points, buy energy-efficient devices, use renewable energy, switch off or use sleep mode.
**Model phrases**: 'This is because...', 'As a result...', 'On the other hand...', 'Overall, the impact is... because...'.
**Avoid** vague words such as 'bad', 'pollution' without saying of what, or 'saves the planet'.
**Time guide**: roughly one minute per mark; for 6 marks aim for 3 to 4 developed points rather than 8 short ones.
**Link to 1.6 context**: always check whether the question asks for environmental issues specifically, not legal or ethical ones.

mistakes.r: State that manufacture, electricity generation, data centres and disposal all cause harm such as carbon dioxide emissions, pollution and e-waste.
mistakes.w: Devices don't harm the environment because they don't make smoke.

mistakes.r: Recycling recovers materials and reduces mining, but it still uses energy and not all e-waste is recycled; reducing and reusing come first.
Cloud data is stored on servers in data centres that use large amounts of electricity and cooling; the impact is moved, not removed.
mistakes.w: The cloud is better for the environment because nothing is physical.

mistakes.r: Give a specific cause and effect, such as 'burning fossil fuels to power devices releases carbon dioxide which contributes to climate change'.
mistakes.w: It is bad for the planet. (no explanation)

mistakes.r: Include benefits such as reduced travel, less paper and smart energy monitoring, then give a justified conclusion.
mistakes.w: Only describing negatives in a 'discuss' question.

mistakes.r: Keep environmental points about resources, energy, pollution and waste; link to ethics only if the question asks.
mistakes.w: Mixing up environmental with ethical or legal issues.

mistakes.r: Say it contains hazardous substances like lead and mercury that can leak into soil and water, and valuable metals that are wasted.
Link each point to the context given, for example a school with 200 tablets or a company with its own servers.
mistakes.w: Ignoring the scenario and giving general facts.

summary: You must understand how digital technology affects the environment: the resources and energy used to make, power and cool devices, the problem of electronic waste, and the ways technology can also reduce environmental harm. It matters because Paper 1 questions ask you to discuss both the damage and the benefits in a given scenario and reach a balanced judgement.

terms.d: The effect that the production, use and disposal of technology has on the natural environment, including land, water, air and climate.
Discarded electrical and electronic equipment, such as old phones, computers and televisions.
The total amount of greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide, released by an activity, product or person.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide, that traps heat in the atmosphere and contributes to climate change.
A resource that exists in a limited quantity and cannot be replaced once used up.
Energy from sources that are naturally replenished, such as wind, solar and hydroelectric power.
A fuel formed from ancient organisms, such as coal, oil and gas, which releases carbon dioxide when burned.
A large facility containing many servers and networking equipment used to store and process data, which uses large amounts of power and cooling.
A site where waste is buried; hazardous chemicals from e-waste can leak from it into soil and water.
Processing used materials so that they can be made into new products, saving raw materials and energy.
Using a device again, by repairing, selling or donating it, rather than throwing it away.
Designing a product so that it becomes outdated or stops working after a limited time, encouraging customers to buy a replacement.
Using less energy to do the same job, for example a device with sleep mode and low-power components.
A low-power state where a device appears off but still uses electricity.
A device that measures a household's energy use and displays it so that people can monitor and reduce it.
Meeting current needs without damaging the environment or reducing the resources available to future generations.

worked.ans: Buying 200 new laptops has an environmental cost because manufacturing uses finite resources such as metals and a lot of energy, which is often generated from fossil fuels and releases carbon dioxide. If the old laptops are thrown away they become e-waste; they contain toxic substances such as lead which can leak from landfill into the soil and water. However, newer laptops may be more energy efficient, so the school will use less electricity, and the old ones can be donated to other schools or recycled so that valuable metals are recovered and less new mining is needed. Overall, the impact can be reduced if the school reuses or recycles the old laptops properly and only replaces those that are really needed, so keeping some of the existing laptops for longer would be best.
worked.q: A school is replacing 200 old laptops. Discuss the environmental impacts of this decision. [6 marks]
steps: Plan a balance: harms of buying new, harms of disposing of old, benefits of the new ones.
Harm 1: manufacturing 200 laptops uses finite metals and a lot of energy, releasing carbon dioxide.
Harm 2: if the old laptops are thrown away they become e-waste, and toxic substances such as lead could leak from landfill.
Benefit 1: newer laptops may be more energy efficient, so electricity use falls.
Benefit 2: the school can donate or recycle the old laptops so metals are recovered and fewer new materials are mined.
Conclusion: the impact depends on whether the old laptops are reused or recycled.

worked.ans: 1. Cloud data is stored on thousands of servers in data centres that run all day and night, so they use large amounts of electricity (1) which, if generated from fossil fuels, releases carbon dioxide (1). 2. The servers produce a lot of heat, so cooling systems are required (1) which use additional electricity and water (1).
worked.q: Explain two ways that using cloud storage can have a negative environmental impact. [4 marks]
steps: Choose two distinct points and give a reason for each.
Point 1: data is held in data centres which contain thousands of servers running constantly, so they use large amounts of electricity.
Point 2: the servers produce heat, so cooling systems are needed which use more electricity and often water.
Add a consequence: if the electricity comes from fossil fuels, carbon dioxide is released.

worked.ans: Energy used = 4380 kWh; cost = £1314 for the year. This shows why running servers all year, plus cooling, has a large energy and environmental cost.
worked.q: A data centre server uses 500 W of power and runs all year (365 days). Electricity costs 30p per kWh. Calculate the energy used and the cost for one year. [3 marks]
steps: Convert watts to kilowatts: 500 W = 0.5 kW.
Hours in a year: 24 x 365 = 8760 hours.
Energy = power x time = 0.5 x 8760 = 4380 kWh.
